title: Pattern Recognition - Mapping Problem Cues to Technique
summary: Fast interviewers aren't smarter in the moment - they're matching a problem's keywords, input shape, and constraint size to a known technique. Build that same cue-to-technique map.

slides.markdown:
Fast interviewers aren't smarter in real time - they're **pattern-matching**. They see "contiguous subarray" and a sliding window lights up before they've consciously analyzed anything. That recognition looks like magic from outside, but it's a learned map from surface cues to technique, built from having solved hundreds of problems that fall into a small number of families.

This topic builds that map explicitly: the keyword cues, the constraint-size cues, and the decision process for picking among the techniques taught across the rest of this area - two pointers, heaps, graphs, DP, greedy, and bit tricks. It doesn't re-teach any of those techniques; it teaches you how to recognize which one a new problem is asking for.

slides.subTitle: The phrases that name a technique
slides.markdown:
Certain phrases in a problem statement map almost directly to a technique family:

- **"Contiguous subarray/substring"** → sliding window. The word "contiguous" is the tell; a non-contiguous subset needs something else entirely.
- **"Kth largest/smallest"** → a heap. Maintaining a running top-k or bottom-k without re-sorting from scratch is what a heap is for.
- **"All combinations/subsets/permutations"** → backtracking. Anything asking you to enumerate every arrangement satisfying a constraint is asking you to build and prune a search tree.

These aren't guarantees - a problem can use "subarray" and still need something else if there's an extra twist - but they're a strong first hypothesis that narrows five techniques down to one before you've read the constraints.

slides.subTitle: Graphs, connectivity, and optimization language
slides.markdown:
More phrase-to-technique mappings, this time from the graph and optimization side:

- **"Shortest path"** → BFS on an unweighted graph, Dijkstra once edges carry weights. The word "shortest" plus "weighted" together should trigger Dijkstra specifically, not BFS.
- **"Connected components" / "are these in the same group"** → Union-Find for incremental grouping queries, or a DFS/BFS sweep if you just need to count components once.
- **"Maximum/minimum over a set of choices"** → DP or greedy. The tell that decides between them is whether an earlier choice can be revisited or must be committed to - covered on the next slide.

Stacking these two slides together: reading "shortest path in a weighted graph with the fewest edge changes" should trigger Dijkstra plus a state-augmented distance array almost immediately, not a blank page.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading the shape before the words
slides.markdown:
Keywords are the fast path, but they can mislead - the more reliable cue is the **shape of the input itself**. Before anything else, ask: is this an array, a tree, a graph, or a string? Each answer narrows which sibling group's toolbox even applies.

An array with a contiguous-range constraint points toward two pointers or sliding window. A tree points toward DFS/BFS traversal or tree DP. A graph with edges and nodes points toward BFS/DFS, Dijkstra, Union-Find, or topological sort depending on what's being asked. A string is often an array in disguise, but character-set-bounded alphabets open up frequency-array tricks that a general array wouldn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Constraint size as a technique filter
slides.markdown:
The stated bound on n doesn't just cap your complexity - it actively rules out entire technique families, which narrows the search before you've matched a single keyword:

| Constraint | What it rules in |
|---|---|
| n ≤ 20 | Bitmask DP, brute-force subsets - exponential is affordable |
| n ≤ 500 | O(n²) DP or graph algorithms like Floyd-Warshall |
| n ≤ 10^5 | O(n log n): sorting-based approaches, heaps, most graph BFS/DFS |
| n ≤ 10^9 | O(log n) or O(1): binary search on the answer, math, two pointers |

A problem with `n ≤ 20` and a phrase like "minimum cost to visit all cities" is a strong bitmask-DP signal specifically *because* of the size bound - the same phrase at `n ≤ 10^5` would need an entirely different approach, since bitmask DP is exponential and would never finish.

slides.subTitle: "Sounds like DP" vs. "actually greedy suffices"
slides.markdown:
Both DP and greedy solve "optimize over a sequence of choices," so they get confused constantly. The tell is a single question: **can an earlier choice be revisited or reconsidered once you see more of the input?**

- **If yes** - a locally good choice can turn out wrong once later elements are known - you need **DP**, because you must keep track of multiple possible states rather than committing early. Longest increasing subsequence is the classic case: the best choice at position i depends on what comes after.
- **If no** - once you've made the locally best choice, it never needs to be undone - **greedy** suffices and is both simpler and faster. Activity selection (always pick the meeting that ends soonest) never needs to reconsider an earlier pick.

When you're not sure which side a problem falls on, try to construct a small counterexample where the greedy choice backfires. If you can build one, it's DP. If you can't, after genuinely trying, that's evidence - not proof - that greedy holds.

slides.sectionTitle: Locking onto the wrong pattern from one word
slides.markdown:
A dangerous version of pattern recognition: hearing a single word like "optimal" or "maximum" and locking onto DP before checking whether the constraints even allow it.

"Find the maximum sum path" sounds like DP by reflex, but if n is bounded at 10^9 with no further structure, an O(n²) DP table is never going to finish in time - the real answer might be a greedy pass or a mathematical closed form that the keyword alone didn't suggest.

The fix is ordering your checks correctly: **read the constraint size before committing to a technique family**, not after. A technique that matches the keyword but violates the size bound is not a candidate at all, no matter how strong the verbal match feels.

slides.sectionTitle: When a problem chains two patterns
slides.markdown:
Many real interview problems aren't a single technique - they're **two patterns chained together**, and missing the second one leaves a technically-working but non-optimal solution.

Common chains: **sort, then two-pointer** - sorting first turns an O(n²) pair-search into something two pointers can do in O(n) - or **hash-map, then sliding window** - a hash map tracks character counts while a window's boundaries move, common in "longest substring with at most k distinct characters" style problems.

Recognizing a chain usually starts with noticing that the first technique you reach for solves *part* of the problem but leaves a sub-problem still unsolved - that leftover sub-problem is where the second pattern lives. Naming both explicitly ("I'll sort first, which lets me two-pointer the rest") is also good narration, tying directly into `thinking-out-loud`.

The opposite failure of locking onto a keyword: **forcing the one technique you're most comfortable with** onto a problem that doesn't actually call for it, because it's the tool you reach for by habit.

Candidates who've drilled DP heavily sometimes DP-table a problem that's actually a straightforward greedy pass, producing correct but needlessly complicated code that also takes longer to write and debug under time pressure. The interviewer notices this as much as they notice a wrong answer - overcomplicating a simple problem reads as a gap in judgment, not a display of skill.

The check is symmetric to the earlier pitfall: after you propose a technique, ask "is there something simpler that also satisfies the constraints?" before you start writing thirty lines of code for a five-line answer.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level habit
slides.markdown:
The cues in this topic are a starting map, not a finished one - the strongest version of this skill comes from **logging your own pattern-to-technique mapping** as you practice, because your personal cue sheet ends up richer than any static list.

After each problem, note which specific phrase or constraint shape led you to the right technique, and just as importantly, note the times a cue misled you and why. Over dozens of problems this becomes closer to instinct than lookup: you read "minimum number of jumps" and a BFS-on-implicit-graph framing surfaces before you've consciously listed the alternatives, the same way "contiguous subarray" now surfaces sliding window without deliberation.

This is also what senior candidates are actually demonstrating when they look fast in an interview - not raw intelligence, but a cue sheet built from more repetitions than a junior candidate has had time to accumulate.

This framework only maps cues to technique families - the techniques themselves live in their own groups: `two-pointers-sliding-window`, `heaps`, `graphs`, `dynamic-programming`, `greedy`, and `bit-manipulation`. If a cue points you toward one of those, that group's content is where the mechanism is actually taught.

Once you've matched a pattern, `complexity-tradeoff-communication` covers stating the resulting time/space trade-off out loud, and `thinking-out-loud` covers narrating the match itself - saying "this reads like a sliding window because the substring has to stay contiguous" is exactly the kind of sentence that turns silent recognition into visible reasoning.
